notes: CPP indefinite suspension appeal; Bennett J applies Stefan/Sadler and dismisses on law-only appeal.

enrichment.short_title: Shanker v GMC: appeal against indefinite performance suspension
key_facts: Dr Shanker, an Indian-qualified GP, faced repeated GMC performance assessments from 2001 showing seriously deficient knowledge and clinical skills.
He practised while suspended at Plumstead, lied to the CPP in 2001, and was convicted of obtaining pecuniary advantage by deception in 2004.
May 2004 reassessment scores remained far below minimum standards and assessors found no insight and that retraining was unlikely to succeed.
The CPP imposed indefinite suspension under section 36A(4); the doctor appealed on questions of law only.
enrichment.procedural_posture: High Court appeal under section 40(5) Medical Act 1983 on questions of law from a Committee on Professional Performance decision.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; indefinite suspension upheld and GMC awarded costs summarily assessed at £5,321.25.
enrichment.ratio: On a section 40(5) appeal the court applies a generous 'question of law' jurisdiction per Stefan v GMC but will defer to the CPP unless findings are unsupported; matters going to character and credibility may be considered for fitness to practise and credibility of evidence without being conflated with performance assessment.
legal_issues: Whether reassessment results justified indefinite suspension
Whether the CPP wrongly took account of character, credibility and honesty
Whether the CPP erred in finding lack of insight
Scope of appellate jurisdiction under section 40(5)
linked_authorities: Stefan v General Medical Council [2002] UKPC 10
Sadler v General Medical Council [2003] UKPC 59
Dr Nandi v General Medical Council [2004] EWHC 2317 (Admin)

notes: Restricted patient recall after insanity acquittal; Keene LJ rejects classification-based limit on section 42(3).

enrichment.short_title: R (AL) v SSHD: lawfulness of recall of conditionally discharged restricted patient
key_facts: AL was acquitted of murder by reason of insanity in 1991 and detained under section 5(1)(a) 1964 Act, treated as restricted under the MHA.
After a conditional discharge in 2001 he formed a relationship with a vulnerable teenager, abused drugs and was recalled in February 2004 on emergency grounds.
Dr Croy's March 2004 report found no mental illness but ongoing psychopathic disorder warranting detention for protection of others.
He challenged continued detention after receipt of that report, arguing recall required the same classified disorder as originally justified detention.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal from refusal of judicial review of Secretary of State recall and interim detention pending MHRT review.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; recall and detention lawful and MHRT referral within one month provided adequate safeguard.
enrichment.ratio: Section 5(1964) detainees are not 'classified' with a particular mental disorder like section 37 patients, so B v Ashworth's treatment-limitation principle does not restrict section 42(3) recall; even for classified patients recall is not limited to the originally specified disorder where public protection requires it.
legal_issues: Whether section 42(3) recall requires the same form of mental disorder as originally classified
Application of R (B) v Ashworth to restricted patients
Whether section 5(1964) orders involve mental disorder classification
Lawfulness of detention between recall and MHRT determination
catchwords: not guilty by reason of insanity
linked_authorities: R (B) v Ashworth Hospital Authority [2003] EWCA Civ 547
Winterwerp v Netherlands (1979) 2 EHRR 387

notes: Gloster J trial of 20 preliminary issues on Stockholm arbitration jurisdiction after Interlife share sale.

enrichment.short_title: SEB Trygg v Manches: Interlife arbitration misnomer and authority issues
key_facts: Arbitration under Stockholm Chamber rules arose from SEB's 1993 purchase of Interlife shares and counterclaim for pension mis-selling indemnities.
Proceedings named Old Aachener Re, which had merged into AMB Generali by universal succession before arbitration began.
Three solicitor firms acted sequentially; AMB contended it was never a party and had not submitted to jurisdiction.
Twenty preliminary liability issues addressed misnomer, actual and ostensible authority, ratification and estoppel.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Commercial Court trial of 20 preliminary issues arising from long-running English-seated Stockholm Chamber arbitration.
enrichment.outcome: AMB held bound to arbitration through misnomer correction, Professor Hauptmann's authority, ratification/acquiescence and estoppel; AMB lost jurisdiction objection; split costs orders made; permission to appeal refused.
enrichment.ratio: Where arbitration is begun against a dissolved vendor company but objectively intended to bind its universal successor, the defect is misnomer not nullity; senior in-house management had authority to commence proceedings and later conduct ratified or estopped denial of party status.
legal_issues: Misnomer versus nullity in arbitration party identification
Actual and ostensible authority under English and German law
Ratification and estoppel by acquiescence
Whether counterclaim service joined AMB to arbitration
linked_authorities: The Sardinia Sulcis [1991] 1 Lloyd's Rep 201
Lazard Brothers v Midland Bank Ltd [1933] AC 289
Nelson v Nelson [1997] 1 WLR 233

notes: Moat House hotel fire certificate sentencing appeal; fines reduced for culpability and profits oversight.

enrichment.short_title: R v ESB Hotels: appeal against fire certificate breach fines after fatal hotel fire
key_facts: Bolton Moat House Hotel, occupied by ESB Hotels Ltd, suffered a corridor fire in April 2001 started by a night porter, killing two elderly guests.
Combustible beds had been stored in a designated means of escape for 12-15 hours despite a fire certificate prohibiting combustibles in corridors.
A February 2001 risk assessment had warned about storing mattresses and beds in inappropriate areas; staff training on removal was inadequate.
Crown Court fines totalled £400,000 plus £11,000 costs for two section 4 offences.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal by leave against Crown Court sentence following guilty pleas committed from magistrates' court.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed in part; fines reduced to £175,000 and £75,000 respectively; defendant's costs order granted.
enrichment.ratio: Foreseeable breach of fire certificate requirements in a sleeping-risk hotel warrants substantial fines even where ignition was criminal employee act, but culpability is reduced where steps were taken to remove obstructions and the judge must have regard to pre-tax profits not merely gross turnover.
legal_issues: Appropriate culpability where employee deliberately started fire
Disparity between fines for related offences
Application of F Howe and Sons and comparable health and safety sentencing cases
Relevance of company financial resources and profit margins
linked_authorities: F Howe and Sons Engineers [1999] 2 Cr App R(S) 37
Colthorp Board Mills Ltd [2002] 2 Cr App R(S) 80
Cardiff City Transport Services [2003] 1 Cr App R(S) 141

notes: Chancery rectification trial; highway adoption hammerhead boundary mistakenly drawn at DD not CC.

enrichment.short_title: James Hay v Cooper Estates: rectification of transfer boundary for adopted highway
key_facts: James Hay pension trustee sold part of Somerset land to Cooper for a retail development with a new adoptable access road.
Parties intended transfer of a hammerhead parcel up to line CC for highway adoption, but contract and transfer plans wrongly showed boundary DD.
Road was built and adopted to CC; Cooper later could block James Hay offering the remainder for adoption.
Cooper denied common intention, contending it acquired only what the transfer described.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Chancery claim for rectification of 1999 transfer and consequential land register correction after trial.
enrichment.outcome: Claim succeeded; common continuing intention and outward accord established; transfer and register ordered rectified to line CC; unjust not to rectify register against adventitious ransom position.
enrichment.ratio: Rectification requires common continuing intention, outward expression of accord and mistake at transfer; Cooper intended to acquire only the turning area required by the highway authority, not the excess shown on the final plan.
legal_issues: Whether James Hay and Cooper shared a common intention as to the transferred parcel
Effect of Bond Pearce letter and B1/138 plan as outward accord
Whether register rectification would be unjust under Schedule 4 LRA 2002
How copying error moved boundary from CC to DD
linked_authorities: Swainland Builders Ltd v Freehold Properties Ltd [2002] EWCA Civ 560

notes: Adverse possession appeal; Rix LJ finds implied licence during 1987-91 sale negotiations.

enrichment.short_title: Dawson v Howard: adverse possession defeated by implied licence pending sale talks
key_facts: Colin Dawson Windows used cleared North End Yard land as a car park from about August 1987.
Mrs Howard claimed paper title to former No 4A, demolished in 1958, identified on a 1958 clearance plan.
From 1987 to August 1991 the parties negotiated purchase; Howard's solicitors permitted occupation unless talks failed.
County court held Dawsons had adversely possessed for twelve years by June 2003 counterclaim.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal from Norwich County Court adverse possession claim and counterclaim for paper title.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; implied licence inferred during negotiations until August 1991 prevented twelve years adverse possession; matter remitted on counterclaim damages.
enrichment.ratio: Possession pending negotiations for purchase of land may be by implied permission; contingent requests to vacate if talks fail do not negate licence, and limitation time does not run while occupation is referable to the owner's permission.
legal_issues: Whether Mrs Howard proved paper title to No 4A
Whether Dawsons' possession was pursuant to an implied licence
Effect of BP Properties v Buckler and Bath DC v Nicholson
Whether Howard had an interest to grant a licence before assent in 2003
linked_authorities: BP Properties Ltd v Buckler (1988) 55 P&CR 337
Bath & North Somerset DC v Nicholson (22 February 2002, unreported)
JA Pye (Oxford) Ltd v Graham [2003] 1 AC 419

notes: Second appeal on shared reservoir grant; downhill owner has priority over Beauchamp.

enrichment.short_title: Mitchell v Potter: construction of shared water rights from hillside reservoir
key_facts: 1986 conveyances split Addiscott Farm, granting the downhill farmland owner rights to draw water from a Stonecross reservoir 'in common' with vendors.
Grant expressly allowed drawing such water as reasonably required for domestic and farm purposes through an existing pipeline.
Defendants contended the uphill owners had first call; claimant sought priority for reasonable requirements.
Deputy District Judge held supply shared with no first call; HHJ Overend reversed, giving claimant priority.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Second appeal on preliminary issue of construction of September 1986 conveyance water rights.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; claimant entitled to draw reasonably required water first, defendants limited to residue; costs reduced slightly.
enrichment.ratio: The phrase 'in common' denotes non-exclusivity but sub-paragraph (ii) grants the downhill owner a positive right to abstract reasonably required water for domestic and farm use, not merely a cap; Beauchamp v Frome is distinguishable on wording and artificial pipe/reservoir context.
legal_issues: Whether water rights are easement or profit à prendre
Priority between uphill and downhill grantees
Construction of 'in common' and 'reasonably required'
Application of Beauchamp v Frome Rural District Council
linked_authorities: Beauchamp v Frome Rural District Council [1938] 1 All ER 595

notes: Abuse of process appeal; Wall LJ strikes out parallel High Court contract claim after ET history.

enrichment.short_title: Enfield v Sivanandan: abuse of process of parallel contract claim after employment tribunal
key_facts: Ms Sivanandan, Enfield's racial equality officer, brought extensive employment tribunal claims including breach of contract from 1997.
Tribunal proceedings were eventually struck out in September 2000 after prolonged adjournments and non-cooperation.
She later issued High Court contract proceedings, obtained default judgment, and asserted she had never accepted dismissal.
Enfield applied to set aside judgment and strike out the claim as abuse of process.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal from High Court refusal to strike out Queen's Bench contract claim following employment tribunal litigation.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; Queen's Bench proceedings struck out under CPR 3.4 as abuse of process; earlier orders set aside.
enrichment.ratio: Where contract and discrimination claims were litigated or available in the employment tribunal and the claimant objectively accepted repudiation by pursuing dismissal remedies, later High Court proceedings repeating the same grievances are an abuse; Henderson v Henderson and Birkett v James principles apply.
legal_issues: Whether breach of contract claim remained before the employment tribunal
Whether High Court claim duplicated tribunal issues
Whether Sivanandan accepted Enfield's repudiation of contract
Application of abuse of process and election principles
linked_authorities: Henderson v Henderson (1843) 3 Hare 100
Johnson v Gore Wood & Co [2002] 2 AC 1
Peyman v Lanjani [2006] EWCA Civ 1212

notes: Asylum certification appeal; Buxton LJ distinguishes refugee and Article 3 grounds under section 96(2)(a).

enrichment.short_title: Borak v SSHD: section 96 certification of fresh asylum claim
key_facts: Croatian Serb Mr Borak claimed asylum from 1999; human rights appeal dismissed June 2002.
Fresh 2003 claim relied on indictment of General Gotovina for murders of claimant's relatives.
Secretary of State certified under section 96(2) preventing appeal as repeating earlier grounds or omitting one-stop evidence.
Administrative Court upheld certification on purposive interpretation of 'ground'.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal from judicial review upholding section 96(2) certification of fresh asylum claim.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed overall; court reversed judge on section 96(2)(a) but upheld certification under section 96(2)(b) for failure to include asylum ground in one-stop statement.
enrichment.ratio: A 'ground' under section 96 comprises both factual and legal elements, so Refugee Convention and Article 3 claims are distinct grounds despite overlapping facts; certification under (b) may apply where new asylum ground should have been included in an earlier one-stop statement even if facts existed but were unknown.
legal_issues: Meaning of 'ground' in section 96(2)(a)
Whether refugee and Article 3 claims are the same ground
Certification where evidence existed but claimant was unaware
Whether Gotovina material should have been in section 75 one-stop statement
linked_authorities: R (Balamurali) v SSHD [2003] EWHC 1183 (Admin)
R (Ullah) v Special Adjudicator [2004] UKHL 26
Secretary of State v Saleem [2000] Imm AR 529
